summary: The note describes the Reformation, which Martin Luther is widely acknowledged to have started with his Ninety-five Theses. Luther criticised the sale of indulgences, papal authority over purgatory, and the doctrine of the merits of the saints. The note says the Protestant Reformation later adopted sola scriptura and sola fide, and that its core motivation was theological, alongside factors such as nationalism, the Western Schism, Curial corruption, humanism and Renaissance learning.
one_line: Overview of the Reformation, its start with Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses, its doctrinal changes, and the factors behind it.
key_facts: Earlier attempts to reform the Catholic Church before Luther included those of Jan Hus, Peter Waldo, and John Wycliffe.
Martin Luther is widely acknowledged to have started the Reformation with the Ninety-five Theses.
Luther began by criticising the sale of indulgences.
Luther insisted that the Pope had no authority over purgatory.
Luther argued that the Catholic doctrine of the merits of the saints had no foundation in the Bible.
The Protestant Reformation incorporated sola scriptura, a complete reliance on Scripture as a source of proper belief.
The Protestant Reformation incorporated sola fide, the belief that faith in Jesus, and not good works, is the only way to obtain God's pardon for sin.
The core motivation behind the Reformation's changes was theological.
Other factors in the Reformation included the rise of nationalism.
The Western Schism eroded loyalty to the Papacy.
The perceived corruption of the Roman Curia was a factor in the Reformation.
The impact of humanism was a factor in the Reformation.
The new learning of the Renaissance questioned much traditional thought.
